sources.shortCitation: Staszic school report for 1915/16 — Przegląd Techniczny, 1917
sources.fullCitation: [Report of the Rada Opiekuńcza and the direction of the Szkoła im. Staszica in Warsaw for the school year 1915/16], Przegląd Techniczny 55 (1917), nos. 23 and 24, p. 187. Stowarzyszenie Techników w Warszawie. Biblioteka Cyfrowa Politechniki Warszawskiej.
sources.researchNote: The report states „Rok szkolny 1915/16 rozpoczęto 6 września” and sets out the intake: 128 new candidates admitted across the school, twelve of them to the fifth class, which then held forty-five pupils out of 309 in all. It also says where the newcomers came from — „przeważnie z opustoszałych szkół państwowych rosyjskich”, mostly from the emptied Russian state schools — which is the position Kaper was in. The twelve are not named, so the report dates the year and not his own first day.
sources.title: Report of the pedagogical council of the Staszic Real School, 1915/16

timelineEvents.title: Transfer to the Staszic Real School
timelineEvents.label: 1915 · Skrynnikov school graduation
timelineEvents.shortDescription: Aged thirteen, Kaper moved from Skrynnikov’s private school to the fifth class of the Staszic Real School, which opened its 1915/16 year on 6 September.
timelineEvents.longDescription: Kaper attended the private school of Aleksander M. Skrynnikov at 49 Żurawia Street, whose curriculum favoured mathematics, the sciences and modern languages over the classical programme of Latin and Greek. Aged thirteen, he transferred to the fifth class of the Stanisław Staszic Real School, which became a state gymnasium in 1918 and where he completed his secondary education. The school’s own report gives the year: it opened on 6 September 1915 and took 128 new candidates, twelve of them into the fifth class, and says they came mostly from the emptied Russian state schools. That is what had happened to Skrynnikov’s: in July 1915 the Russian state and private secondary schools of Warsaw were evacuated into Russia with their staff, most of their pupils and their equipment, Skrynnikov’s being assigned Moscow, and the German army took the school buildings on entering the city on 5 August. The report does not name the twelve, so the year has a first day and Kaper’s own does not.
